title: Conclusion
text: Delivery time on Olist is driven mainly by route: where the seller is, where the customer is, and whether the two are in the same state. Product and order characteristics add a smaller amount, and purchase timing adds less than route, although the slow months matter: in the scenarios below, a November order takes several days longer than an August order on the same route. The best model (Decision Tree on R3 + Olist estimate) predicts delivery time on unseen orders to within about 4.8 days on average and explains about 31% of the variation, using only information available at or shortly after checkout. That is 24% lower error than always predicting the average (6.3 days), and 9% lower than the first-draft model (5.2 days), which used fewer features (it was refit on the same order-grouped split, so the comparison is fair). Olist’s own checkout estimate is much looser: on its own it explains only 15% of the variation, and on the test orders it is on average 11.5 days longer than what actually happened. What follows turns those findings into concrete order scenarios and recommendations.

text:
Six order scenarios, predicted
To make the model concrete, we score six “typical order” profiles. For each one we take real training orders on that route (seller state to customer state), use their median freight, weight, price, size, and Olist estimate, and set the purchase month. August is a fast month in the exploration, and November is a slow one. Both the lasso (the interpretable linear model) and the decision tree (the most accurate model) score each profile.


Code
# Most common category among a route's orders
mode_level <- function(x) {
  tab <- table(as.character(x))
  x[which(as.character(x) == names(which.max(tab)))[1]]
}

# A "typical order" on a route: median values for numeric fields and the most common
# category for the rest, taken from real training orders, with the purchase month set explicitly
build_scenario <- function(label, seller, cust, month) {
  rows <- train |> filter(seller_state == seller, customer_state == cust)
  stopifnot(nrow(rows) > 0)

  rows |>
    summarise(
      across(where(is.numeric), \(x) median(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
      across(where(is.factor), mode_level)
    ) |>
    select(-delivery_days) |>
    mutate(
      order_id = "scenario",
      purchase_month = factor(as.character(month), levels = levels(train$purchase_month)),
      label = label,
      n_similar = nrow(rows),
      route_median_days = median(rows$delivery_days)
    )
}

title: Conclusion
section: What the team should do
text:
What the team should do

Make the delivery promise route-aware. Set the checkout estimate from seller state, customer state, and month, instead of one rule for everything. The tier table shows how unevenly the current estimate is padded (9.9 days on Same state, 16 days on Cross-state to North). Same-state routes are the natural first pilot: they are the most predictable tier (average miss of 3.3 days) and today’s estimate there is 17.3 days against 7.3 actual. The buffer should be chosen so the late rate stays at or below today’s 5.1% on that tier. A pilot on a few routes would show how many days could be saved. Measure it by: average promised days and the late rate, by route tier.
Show a delivery window, not a single date. Point predictions are good on average but miss the slow tail, and the width of the uncertainty depends on the route (about 10 days on the tightest tier and 23 days on Cross-state to North, measured as the middle 80% of outcomes). Offering “between day X and day Y” is more honest and matches how the model behaves. Measure it by: the share of orders that land inside the window, which should be close to the 80% it is designed for.
Add a seasonal buffer for the slow months. Orders placed in Mar, Nov, Feb are late most often. Extend the promise or add carrier capacity in those months. Check whether the pattern holds in newer data before committing. Measure it by: the late rate in those months, year over year.
Treat the north and northeast as a separate service tier. Routes into these regions are the slowest and the hardest to predict (the highest-error tier is Cross-state to North, with an average miss of 8 days). Set separate expectations, review carrier performance on these lanes, and consider whether stocking inventory closer to these customers is worth testing. Measure it by: delivery time and prediction error on these lanes, tracked separately.
Test whether sourcing closer to the buyer helps. Same-state routes are the fastest, and the same-state flag is among the most important features in the tree (second only to customer state). That is an association, not proof that moving a seller would change delivery time, because sellers and buyers in the same state may also differ in carrier mix and product type. A small pilot, such as a “ships from your state” badge or search ranking, would show whether the effect is real. Measure it by: conversion and delivery time on the pilot group against a control.
Do not spend effort on purchase weekday or time of day. In the Exploration page, weekday moved average delivery time by under two days and time of day by well under a day, against a gap of about a week between same-state and cross-state routes. Put effort into route, carrier, and seller handling instead.
Look at seller handling time. The shipping deadline the seller was given (ship_window_days) is a predictor in the models, and the Exploration page shows median delivery time differing across shipping-window groups. We cannot tell from this data whether sellers who are given more time actually take more time, so this is a question to investigate with seller-level shipping timestamps.
Keep the model honest over time. Retrain on recent orders at a regular interval, watch average error by route tier, and treat a sustained rise in error as a sign that carrier performance or demand has shifted.

title: Conclusion
section: How far to trust it
text:
How far to trust it

Accuracy is useful, not exact. A typical miss is about 4.8 days, and the average error is much smaller than the error on the worst orders (RMSE 7.6 days). This is good for checkout windows and capacity planning, not for day-exact commitments.
The slow tail is still hard. The model under-predicts the slowest orders, because it predicts a typical value for a right-skewed target. That is why we recommend a window with a buffer.
A random split tests similar orders, not future ones. The test orders come from the same 2016 to 2018 period as the training orders. The model has not been tested on a new carrier contract, a strike, or a different year.
Single test set. Differences of a few hundredths of a day between models are not meaningful.
Order-item grain. delivery_days is an order-level duration repeated across the items of an order, so multi-item orders carry slightly more weight in the metrics.
Associations, not causes. The importance scores and coefficients show what the models rely on to predict. They do not show what causes a delay, which is why recommendations 5 and 7 are framed as tests.
Coarse geography. Zip-code region is only a rough stand-in for distance, and the scenarios use median values for each route.

title: Conclusion
section: What would improve it next
text:
What would improve it next

Real seller-to-customer distance from Olist’s geolocation table, which is the most promising feature not yet used.
Stage-level timestamps (approval, handoff to carrier, delivery), so seller handling time and carrier transit time can be modelled separately and each team can see its own share.
A time-based test: train on earlier months and test on later ones, which is a stricter check than a random split.
Non-linear ensemble models and a log-transformed target. These were outside the scope here and were not tested on the order-grouped split. They might lower typical error, at the cost of being harder to explain.

title: Exploration
section: The question, the target, and the decision
text:
The question, the target, and the decision
Business question. What drives the number of days an Olist order takes to reach the customer, and can Olist predict that number at checkout well enough to show customers a more accurate delivery estimate?
Target. The one outcome used throughout this project is delivery_days: the days from the order purchase to delivery at the customer’s address. It is a number, it is only known after delivery, and it is what the models on the Modeling page predict.
What Olist would do differently. At checkout, Olist shows an estimated delivery date. If that estimate is much longer than real delivery times, customers see slower service than they actually get. If it is too short, orders arrive late. A route-aware prediction of delivery_days lets Olist set estimates that are tighter where deliveries are fast and still safe where they are slow.
Why delivery_days and not “late or on time”. Only 7.4% of items arrive after Olist’s estimated date, while 91.2% arrive before it and 1.4% arrive on the day. With so few late items there is little to predict in a late-or-not outcome, whereas delivery_days varies a lot across routes, products, and months.
In short. Items shipped inside one state average 7.5 days, against 14.6 days when seller and customer are in different states, a gap of 7.1 days. Olist’s checkout estimate is on average 11.4 days longer than the actual delivery.
How this page is organized. We look at the target on its own (Section 1), check the data decisions that could distort it (Section 2), profile the columns (Section 3), compare groups in tables (Section 4), draw the relationships that matter (Section 5), and close with findings, a decision, and limitations (Section 6). Counts are order items unless a sentence says “orders”.

5. What do the relationships look like?
The tables compared averages. These charts show the relationships behind them, each with the expectation stated first.

5.1 How much does the route matter?
Expectation. For each seller state, items delivered inside the same state (for example SP to SP) should be the fastest, and states far from the seller should be slower.


Show code

top_cust   <- olist |> count(customer_state, sort = TRUE) |> slice_head(n = 10) |> pull(customer_state)

heat <- olist |>
  filter(seller_state %in% top_seller, customer_state %in% top_cust) |>
  group_by(seller_state, customer_state) |>
  summarise(n = n(), avg_days = mean(delivery_days), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(n >= 30) |>
  mutate(
    customer_state = factor(customer_state, levels = top_cust),
    seller_state = factor(seller_state, levels = rev(top_seller))
  )

ggplot(heat, aes(x = customer_state, y = seller_state, fill = avg_days)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(avg_days)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "#deebf7", high = "#08519c", name = "Average\ndelivery days") +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Same-state items average ", num(same$actual), " days, against ",
                   num(cross$actual), " days across states"),
    x = "Customer state (ten largest)", y = "Seller state (six largest)"
  )

slow_cell <- heat |> slice_max(avg_days, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)








Figure 2: Average delivery days by seller state and customer state (largest states; cells with fewer than 30 items are left blank)





The slowest cell shown is PR to BA at 21 days (from 163 items). Reading across any row, delivery time changes strongly with the customer’s state, so where the item travels is a large part of what determines how long it takes.


5.2 Is delivery time stable over time?
Expectation. If delivery performance is stable, the average should stay flat across months. Visible swings would mean that purchase month, or the year, needs to be in the model.


Show code
monthly_all <- olist |>
  group_by(purchase_year_month) |>
  summarise(n = n(), avg_days = mean(delivery_days),
            late_pct = 100 * mean(delivery_days > estimated_days), .groups = "drop")

n_months_dropped <- sum(monthly_all$n < 100)
monthly <- monthly_all |> filter(n >= 100)

peak_month <- monthly |> slice_max(avg_days, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)
low_month  <- monthly |> slice_min(avg_days, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

monthly |>
  pivot_longer(c(avg_days, late_pct), names_to = "measure", values_to = "value") |>
  mutate(measure = recode(measure,
                          avg_days = "Average delivery days",
                          late_pct = "Items later than Olist's estimate (%)")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = purchase_year_month, y = value)) +
  geom_line(color = blue, linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(color = blue) +
  facet_wrap(~measure, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "3 months", date_labels = "%b %Y") +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Delivery time peaked in ", format(peak_month$purchase_year_month, "%B %Y"),
                   " at ", num(peak_month$avg_days), " days; the low was ",
                   num(low_month$avg_days), " days"),
    x = "Purchase month", y = NULL
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))








Figure 3: Average delivery days and share of items later than Olist’s estimate, by purchase month (months with at least 100 items)





Delivery time moves by 11.8 days between the slowest month (October 2016) and the fastest (August 2018), so the average is not stable over time. 2 months with fewer than 100 items (the first and last months of the data) are left out of the chart. Plausible explanations are holiday and promotion demand (for example Black Friday and Christmas) and the platform’s rapid growth in 2017 and 2018, which may have strained delivery capacity; this data cannot separate them. The slow months in the table in Section 4.5 fall in the Brazilian summer, so cold weather cannot be the explanation. The practical point is that purchase month and year both carry information.


5.3 How far is Olist’s estimate from reality?
Expectation. If Olist’s estimates were accurate, items would sit on the diagonal. Items below the diagonal arrive earlier than estimated.


Show code
ggplot(olist, aes(x = estimated_days, y = delivery_days)) +
  geom_bin2d(binwidth = c(2, 2)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = orange, linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10", name = "Order items") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 60), ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(
    title = paste0(pct0(share_early), " of items arrive before Olist's estimated date"),
    x = "Olist's estimated delivery days (at checkout)",
    y = "Actual delivery days"
  )








Figure 4: Olist’s estimated delivery days against actual delivery days (darker = more items; dashed line = estimate equals actual)





Most of the mass lies below the diagonal. The estimate is on average 11.4 days longer than the actual delivery, and on same-state routes 52% of items arrive at least 10 days before the estimated date (against 67% on cross-state routes). The estimate does rise with actual delivery time, so it contains route information. It is padded on both route types: the average estimate is 17.3 days against 7.5 actual on same-state routes (9.9 days of padding) and 26.9 against 14.6 on cross-state routes (12.3 days). Cross-state routes carry more padding in absolute days and in the share of items arriving 10 or more days early.


5.4 Do handling time and order size matter?
Expectation. A longer seller shipping window should mean a later hand-off to the carrier, and orders with several items or several sellers should take longer because parts ship separately.


Show code
handling <- bind_rows(
  olist |> mutate(group = "Shipping window",
                  level = cut(ship_window_days, c(-Inf, 3, 5, 7, 10, Inf),
                              labels = c("3 days or less", "4-5", "6-7", "8-10", "Over 10"))),
  olist |> mutate(group = "Items per order",
                  level = cut(n_items, c(0, 1, 2, Inf), labels = c("1", "2", "3 or more"))),
  olist |> mutate(group = "Sellers per order",
                  level = cut(n_sellers, c(0, 1, Inf), labels = c("1", "2 or more")))
) |>
  filter(!is.na(level)) |>
  group_by(group, level) |>
  summarise(n = n(), med = median(delivery_days),
            q25 = quantile(delivery_days, 0.25), q75 = quantile(delivery_days, 0.75),
            .groups = "drop")

ggplot(handling, aes(x = level, y = med)) +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = q25, ymax = q75), color = blue) +
  facet_wrap(~group, scales = "free_x") +
  labs(
    title = "Handling time and order size move delivery time, but less than route does",
    x = NULL, y = "Median delivery days (bars: 25th to 75th percentile)"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

multi_seller <- handling |> filter(group == "Sellers per order")
sw <- handling |> filter(group == "Shipping window")








Figure 5: Delivery days by seller shipping window, items per order, and sellers per order (medians with the middle 50% of items)





Orders with two or more sellers have a median of 7 days against 10 for single-seller orders, the opposite of what we expected; the data cannot say why, and it may reflect which sellers and routes these orders involve. Across shipping-window groups the median runs from 6 to 14 days. The shipping window is a deadline the seller was given, not the time the seller actually took, so its link to delivery time is indirect. These features are kept in the models, but they matter less than route.


5.5 Does freight signal slower delivery?
Expectation. Freight should rise with package weight. Slower, longer routes should also cost more to ship, so items with higher freight should take longer to arrive.


Show code
pos_weight <- olist |> filter(!is.na(product_weight_g), product_weight_g > 0)
rho <- cor(pos_weight$product_weight_g, pos_weight$freight_value, method = "spearman")
rho_word <- if (abs(rho) >= 0.5) "strongly" else if (abs(rho) >= 0.3) "moderately" else "weakly"

olist |>
  filter(product_weight_g > 0, freight_value > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = product_weight_g, y = freight_value)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 50) +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10", name = "Order items") +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Freight is ", rho_word, " related to weight (rank correlation ", num(rho, 2), ")"),
    x = "Product weight (g, log scale)", y = "Freight value (R$, log scale)"
  )








Figure 6: Freight value against product weight (both on log scales; darker = more items)







Show code
freight_bands <- olist |>
  mutate(band = ntile(freight_value, 5)) |>
  group_by(band) |>
  mutate(band_label = paste0("R$ ", round(min(freight_value)), " to ", round(max(freight_value)))) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(band_label = fct_reorder(band_label, band))

band_med <- freight_bands |>
  group_by(band) |>
  summarise(med = median(delivery_days), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(freight_bands, aes(x = band_label, y = delivery_days)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#9ecae1", outlier.alpha = 0.1) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 60)) +
  labs(
    title = paste0("Median delivery time moves from ", band_med$med[1], " to ",
                   band_med$med[5], " days across freight bands"),
    x = "Freight band", y = "Delivery days"
  )








Figure 7: Delivery days by freight band (five equal-sized groups of items; outliers faded)





Weight explains part of freight, with wide spread, so freight also reflects distance and package size. Freight and delivery time are linked: the median delivery time is 5 days in the cheapest freight band and 13 days in the most expensive. Freight is a useful predictor, but it is probably a stand-in for how far the item travels.

title: Exploration
section: 6. What did we learn, and what do we do with it?
text:
6. What did we learn, and what do we do with it?

Key findings

Delivery time is right-skewed. The median is 10 days and the average 12.0, with a tail to 209 days. A small share of very slow items drives the gap.
Route is the strongest separator. Same-state items average 7.5 days, against 14.6 days across states, and the heatmap shows delivery time changing strongly with the customer’s state.
Purchase month matters, weekday and time of day matter little. Months differ by 7.2 days, while weekday and time of day differ by 1.7 and 0.2 days.
Olist’s estimates are padded on both route types, more across states. 91% of items arrive before the estimated date and only 7% after it. At least 10 days early: 52% of same-state items and 67% of cross-state items.
Handling and order size matter less than route. The median moves from 6 to 14 days across shipping-window groups, and multi-seller orders are not slower than single-seller orders.
Package attributes add less than route. Freight is linked to delivery time, partly because it reflects distance, while price, weight, and volume have weak straight-line correlations with it.



Decision for Olist
Pilot a route-aware checkout estimate, starting with same-state routes. Same-state routes are the most consistent (SD 6.3 days against 10.0 across states), so a tighter estimate there carries the least risk of late orders. Same-state items arrive in 7.5 days on average against an average estimate of 17.3 days. Cross-state routes carry more padding (12.3 days against 9.9), so they are the larger prize, to take on once the same-state pilot shows the late share holds. A prediction of delivery_days based on seller state, customer state, and purchase month could tighten these estimates. Judge the pilot by two numbers: the average promised days, which should fall, and the share of late items, which should not rise above today’s 7.4%.


Limitations

Orders with a delivery date only. Items with no delivery date are excluded, and the seven canceled items that do have one remain, so the data says nothing about orders that were never delivered or were lost.
Partial years. The data covers 2016 to 2018, with partial years at both ends, so month and year effects overlap.
Pooled before the split. This exploration describes all items before the train/test split on the Modeling page. It only summarizes patterns and nothing from it is fed into the models, but the group averages here include rows that later become test rows.
One row per item. Orders with several items count several times, so multi-item orders carry more weight in the averages.
Coarse geography. State and region are rough stand-ins for distance, and the data has no carrier or weather information.
Unused tables. The payments and reviews tables are not used in this analysis.
Associations only. Every comparison here describes patterns, not causes.



What does this mean for the models?

Target. Keep delivery_days on its raw scale, so errors are in days, and report MAE alongside RMSE because of the long tail.
Leakage. delayed_days, delivered_status, order_status, and the delivery date are known only after delivery and are excluded from the predictors.
Features to build. Same-state route flag, regions, package volume and density, seller shipping window, and items and sellers per order.
States. Small states are the slowest destinations, so they are not merged into an “other” group.
Timing. Purchase month and year are treated as categories because their effect is not a straight line.
Benchmarks. Compare against always predicting the average, and against Olist’s own estimate.

title: Home
section: Why this matters
text:
Why this matters
Olist is a Brazilian online marketplace that connects small sellers to customers across the country. At checkout it shows an estimated delivery date: too long, and customers see slower service than they get; too short, and orders arrive late. A route-aware prediction of delivery_days would let Olist tighten estimates where deliveries are fast and keep them safe where they are slow. The data covers 110,196 order items from 96,476 orders (2016 to 2018).

title: Home
section: Key takeaways
text:
Key takeaways

Exploration: route matters most. Same-state items average 7.5 days against 14.6 across states, and Olist’s estimate is 11.4 days longer than actual on average (91% of items arrive early, 7% late).
Modeling: on unseen orders, the best model (a decision tree) is off by about 4.8 days on average, against 6.3 for always guessing the average and 5.5 for Olist’s estimate alone. Simpler linear models come close.
Decision: pilot a route-aware checkout estimate, starting with same-state routes, and judge it by falling average promised days without a rise in the 7% late share.

Step 5: Saving the Cleaned Dataset and Next Step
Saves the cleaned df_master dataset to data/df_master_clean.rds so downstream pages load a consistent, validated dataset. The numeric product fields are still unfilled at this point.
With df_master_clean.rds saved, the Exploration page examines delivery_days directly first, then tests relationships across geography, purchase month, shipping cost, and product characteristics before closing with a data backed decision and limitations.

title: Modeling
text:
This analysis builds models that predict delivery_days (days from order purchase to customer delivery) using only information that is available when an order is placed or approved. It starts from the cleaned order-item dataset prepared on the Data page, engineers route, product, and timing features, and compares three feature recipes across four model families, plus benchmarks, on a held-out test set.
Design choices

Split by order, not by row. The data has one row per order item, and delivery_days repeats across the items of an order. If items from one order landed in both training and test data, the test score would be inflated. Every split below keeps all items of an order together.
Train / validation / test, no cross-validation. Model settings are chosen on a validation set carved out of the training data. The test set is used once, at the end.
Three recipes that add one group of features at a time, so we can see what each group contributes.
Four model families: linear regression, ridge, lasso, and a decision tree.
Metrics in days. We keep delivery_days on its raw scale so errors are directly interpretable. MAE (average absolute error) is the primary metric, RMSE (which penalizes large misses more) is secondary, and R² is the traditional version, 1 - SSE/SST on the test set. An R² of 0 means no better than predicting the average; it can be negative.

What was kept out of the predictors, and why

We build features in four groups: route (where the item travels), timing, product and order characteristics, and Olist’s own checkout estimate.


Code
df_model <- df_clean |>
  # Order size: how many items, and how many different sellers, share one order
  group_by(order_id) |>
  mutate(n_items = n(), n_sellers = n_distinct(seller_id)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    # Handling time the seller was given before the item had to ship
    ship_window_days = as.numeric(difftime(shipping_limit_date,
                                           order_purchase_timestamp, units = "days")),
    # Package size, density, and shipping cost relative to item value
    volume_cm3    = product_length_cm * product_height_cm * product_width_cm,
    density_g_cm3 = product_weight_g / pmax(volume_cm3, 1),
    freight_ratio = freight_value / price,
    # Route features. Coordinates are not available, so distance is approximated by a
    # same-state flag and by the first digit of the zip prefix (a coarse geographic region)
    same_state    = factor(if_else(seller_state == customer_state, "same", "different")),
    cust_region   = factor(substr(sprintf("%05d", as.integer(customer_zip_code_prefix)), 1, 1)),
    seller_region = factor(substr(sprintf("%05d", as.integer(seller_zip_code_prefix)), 1, 1)),
    same_region   = factor(if_else(cust_region == seller_region, "same", "different")),
    # Timing and category fields are treated as categories, because seasonality
    # (for example a slow month) is not a straight-line effect
    purchase_year  = factor(purchase_year),
    purchase_month = factor(purchase_month),
    purchase_dow   = factor(purchase_day_of_week),
    customer_state = factor(customer_state),
    seller_state   = factor(seller_state),
    category       = factor(product_category_name_english)
  ) |>
  select(order_id, delivery_days, estimated_days,
         customer_state, seller_state, same_state, cust_region, seller_region,
         same_region, purchase_year, purchase_month, purchase_dow,

We hold out 20% of orders as the test set. From the remaining training orders, we hold out a further 20% as a validation set, used only to choose model settings. Both splits are grouped by order_id, and a check confirms that no order appears on both sides of a split.

# Split by order, not by row: every item of an order goes to the same set, so the
# test score is not inflated by near-duplicate rows from the same order
set.seed(123)
split <- group_initial_split(df_model, group = order_id, prop = 0.8)
train <- training(split)
test  <- testing(split)

# Validation set: a slice of the training orders used only to choose model settings,
# so the test set stays untouched until the final scoring
inner     <- group_initial_split(train, group = order_id, prop = 0.8)
train_sub <- training(inner)
val       <- testing(inner)

  check = c("Orders in both train and test", "Orders in both train-sub and validation"),
  overlapping_orders = c(

    length(intersect(train_sub$order_id, val$order_id))

make_recipe <- function(preds) {
  rec <- recipe(delivery_days ~ .,
                data = train |> select(delivery_days, order_id, all_of(preds))) |>
    # order_id only identifies the order; it is not a predictor
    update_role(order_id, new_role = "id") |>
    # A category first seen after training gets its own level instead of causing an error
    step_novel(all_nominal_predictors())
  # Rare product categories (under 1% of rows) are pooled; states are deliberately not pooled
  # because the smallest states are the slowest destinations
  if ("category" %in% preds) rec <- rec |> step_other(category, threshold = 0.01)
  rec |>
    # Each category becomes a 0/1 indicator column
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    # Drop constant columns, and columns that duplicate other columns exactly
    step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_lincomb(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    # Put every numeric predictor on the same scale so penalties treat them evenly
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
}

Every recipe applies the same preprocessing: unseen category levels are handled with step_novel(), product categories below 1% of rows are grouped (only in recipes that include category), categorical variables are dummy-encoded, constant and redundant columns are removed, missing numeric product fields (left unfilled on the Data page) are imputed with the median of the training rows only, and numeric predictors are standardized. All of it is learned from the training data inside a workflow, never from the test set.



Benchmarks give the models something to beat:

Naive: always predict the average training delivery time.
Olist estimate only: a one-variable linear model on estimated_days.
First-draft ridge: the ridge model from the project’s first modeling iteration (freight, weight, state, and purchase month), refit on the same grouped split so the comparison is fair.

Models: linear regression (no settings), ridge and lasso (one setting each, the penalty), and a decision tree (depth and minimum node size). The penalty and tree settings are chosen as follows: fit each candidate on the training sub-sample, measure MAE on the validation set, and keep the candidate with the lowest validation MAE. The chosen settings are then refit on the full training data and scored once on the test set.


Code
# Metrics: RMSE and MAE in days, and traditional R-squared (1 - SSE/SST)
mset <- metric_set(rmse, mae, rsq_trad)

fit_wf <- function(rec, spec, data) {
  workflow() |> add_recipe(rec) |> add_model(spec) |> fit(data)
}
# Average absolute error in days on a dataset; used to compare candidate settings
mae_on <- function(fit, data) {
  predict(fit, new_data = data) |>
    bind_cols(data |> select(delivery_days)) |>
    mae(truth = delivery_days, estimate = .pred) |>
    pull(.estimate)
}
score_fit <- function(fit) {
  predict(fit, new_data = test) |>
    bind_cols(test |> select(delivery_days)) |>
    mset(truth = delivery_days, estimate = .pred)
}

glmnet_spec <- function(p, mixture) {
  linear_reg(penalty = p, mixture = mixture) |> set_engine("glmnet")
}
# cost_complexity is fixed at a small value, so depth and minimum node size control tree complexity
tree_spec <- function(d, m) {
  decision_tree(tree_depth = d, min_n = m, cost_complexity = 0.0001) |>
    set_engine("rpart") |> set_mode("regression")
}

# Candidate settings: penalties from very weak (1e-5) to strong (1), and six tree shapes
pen_grid  <- 10^seq(-5, 0, length.out = 10)
tree_grid <- expand_grid(tree_depth = c(5, 8, 12), min_n = c(20, 60))

# Fit each candidate on the training sub-sample and keep the one with the lowest validation MAE
tune_pen <- function(rec, mixture) {
  maes <- map_dbl(pen_grid, \(p) fit_wf(rec, glmnet_spec(p, mixture), train_sub) |> mae_on(val))
  pen_grid[which.min(maes)]
}
tune_tree <- function(rec) {
  maes <- pmap_dbl(tree_grid, \(tree_depth, min_n)
                   fit_wf(rec, tree_spec(tree_depth, min_n), train_sub) |> mae_on(val))
  tree_grid[which.min(maes), ]

Code
cache_file <- "data/modeling_cache.rds"

if (file.exists(cache_file)) {
  cache <- read_rds(cache_file)
} else {
  # Benchmarks: simple reference points that every model has to beat
  bench_naive <- test |>
    mutate(.pred = mean(train$delivery_days)) |>
    mset(truth = delivery_days, estimate = .pred) |>
    mutate(recipe = "Benchmark", model = "Naive (train mean)", settings = "")

  fit_olist <- fit_wf(recipe(delivery_days ~ estimated_days, data = train),
                      linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"), train)
  bench_olist <- score_fit(fit_olist) |>
    mutate(recipe = "Benchmark", model = "Olist estimate only (LM)", settings = "")

  # First-draft model: the original small feature set, refit on the same grouped split
  rec_orig <- recipe(delivery_days ~ freight_value + product_weight_g +
                       customer_state + seller_state + purchase_month,
                     data = train) |>
    step_other(all_nominal_predictors(), threshold = 0.02) |>
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
  fit_orig <- fit_wf(rec_orig, glmnet_spec(0.1, 0), train)
  bench_orig <- score_fit(fit_orig) |>
    mutate(recipe = "Benchmark", model = "First-draft ridge (original features)",
           settings = "penalty=0.1")

  # Fit all four model families on each recipe. Settings are chosen on the validation set,
  # then the final models are refit on the full training data
  run_recipe <- function(preds, rec_name) {
    rec   <- make_recipe(preds)
    pen_r <- tune_pen(rec, 0)
    pen_l <- tune_pen(rec, 1)
    bt    <- tune_tree(rec)

    fits <- list(
      "Linear Regression" = fit_wf(rec, linear_reg() |> set_engine("lm"), train),
      "Ridge"             = fit_wf(rec, glmnet_spec(pen_r, 0), train),
      "Lasso"             = fit_wf(rec, glmnet_spec(pen_l, 1), train),
      "Decision Tree"     = fit_wf(rec, tree_spec(bt$tree_depth, bt$min_n), train)
    )
    settings <- c(
      "Linear Regression" = "none",
      "Ridge"             = paste0("penalty=", signif(pen_r, 2)),
      "Lasso"             = paste0("penalty=", signif(pen_l, 2)),
      "Decision Tree"     = paste0("depth=", bt$tree_depth, ", min_n=", bt$min_n)
    )

    list(
      metrics = imap(fits, \(fit, model_name)
                     score_fit(fit) |>
                       mutate(recipe = rec_name, model = model_name,
                              settings = settings[[model_name]])) |>
        list_rbind(),
      fits = fits[c("Lasso", "Decision Tree")]
    )
  }

  runs <- imap(recipe_defs, run_recipe)

  cache <- list(
    results_all = bind_rows(bench_naive, bench_olist, bench_orig,
                            map(runs, "metrics") |> list_rbind()),
    fit_lasso3  = runs[["R3 + Olist estimate"]]$fits[["Lasso"]],
    fit_tree3   = runs[["R3 + Olist estimate"]]$fits[["Decision Tree"]]
  )
  write_rds(cache, cache_file)
}

Best configuration: Decision Tree on R3 + Olist estimate, with a test MAE of 4.79 days, RMSE of 7.61 days, and R² of 0.31. In plain terms, using only information available at or shortly after checkout, the model explains about 31% of the variation in delivery time, with a typical miss of about 4.8 days.
Improvement over the benchmarks: MAE is 24% lower than always predicting the average (6.31 days), and 9% lower than the first-draft ridge (5.25 days; R² 0.24) on the same grouped split.
Features matter more than model choice. For linear regression, adding product and order features (R1 to R2) lowers MAE from 5.01 to 4.87 days. That estimate is weak on its own (R² of 0.15), and its route information is largely redundant with the state and region features already in the model.
Regularization made almost no difference. In Recipe 3, linear regression, ridge, and lasso have RMSEs between 7.59 and 7.6 days. title: Modeling
text:
We build features in four groups: route (where the item travels), timing, product and order characteristics, and Olist’s own checkout estimate.


Code
df_model <- df_clean |>
  # Order size: how many items, and how many different sellers, share one order
  group_by(order_id) |>
  mutate(n_items = n(), n_sellers = n_distinct(seller_id)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  mutate(
    # Handling time the seller was given before the item had to ship
    ship_window_days = as.numeric(difftime(shipping_limit_date,
                                           order_purchase_timestamp, units = "days")),
    # Package size, density, and shipping cost relative to item value
    volume_cm3    = product_length_cm * product_height_cm * product_width_cm,
    density_g_cm3 = product_weight_g / pmax(volume_cm3, 1),
    freight_ratio = freight_value / price,
    # Route features. Coordinates are not available, so distance is approximated by a
    # same-state flag and by the first digit of the zip prefix (a coarse geographic region)
    same_state    = factor(if_else(seller_state == customer_state, "same", "different")),
    cust_region   = factor(substr(sprintf("%05d", as.integer(customer_zip_code_prefix)), 1, 1)),
    seller_region = factor(substr(sprintf("%05d", as.integer(seller_zip_code_prefix)), 1, 1)),
    same_region   = factor(if_else(cust_region == seller_region, "same", "different")),
    # Timing and category fields are treated as categories, because seasonality
    # (for example a slow month) is not a straight-line effect
    purchase_year  = factor(purchase_year),
    purchase_month = factor(purchase_month),
    purchase_dow   = factor(purchase_day_of_week),
    customer_state = factor(customer_state),
    seller_state   = factor(seller_state),
    category       = factor(product_category_name_english)

         customer_state, seller_state, same_state, cust_region, seller_region,

text:
Each recipe adds one group of predictors to the previous one. Comparing them shows what each group is worth.


Code
# Predictor groups. Each recipe adds one group to the one before it, so the
# improvement from each group of features can be measured on its own
preds_geo <- c("customer_state", "seller_state", "same_state", "cust_region",
               "seller_region", "same_region", "purchase_year",
               "purchase_month", "purchase_dow")

preds_prod <- c("freight_value", "price", "freight_ratio", "product_weight_g",
                "volume_cm3", "density_g_cm3", "n_items", "n_sellers",
                "ship_window_days", "category", "product_photos_qty",
                "product_name_length", "product_description_length")

recipe_defs <- list(
  "R1 Geography + timing" = preds_geo,
  "R2 + Product & order"  = c(preds_geo, preds_prod),
  "R3 + Olist estimate"   = c(preds_geo, preds_prod, "estimated_days")
)

make_recipe <- function(preds) {
  rec <- recipe(delivery_days ~ .,
                data = train |> select(delivery_days, order_id, all_of(preds))) |>
    # order_id only identifies the order; it is not a predictor
    update_role(order_id, new_role = "id") |>
    # A category first seen after training gets its own level instead of causing an error
    step_novel(all_nominal_predictors())
  # Rare product categories (under 1% of rows) are pooled; states are deliberately not pooled
  # because the smallest states are the slowest destinations
  if ("category" %in% preds) rec <- rec |> step_other(category, threshold = 0.01)
  rec |>
    # Each category becomes a 0/1 indicator column
    step_dummy(all_nominal_predictors()) |>
    # Drop constant columns, and columns that duplicate other columns exactly
    step_zv(all_predictors()) |>
    step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    step_lincomb(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
    # Put every numeric predictor on the same scale so penalties treat them evenly
    step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())
}

    str_detect(term, "^customer_state") ~ "customer_state",
    str_detect(term, "^seller_state")   ~ "seller_state",
    str_detect(term, "^same_state")     ~ "same_state",
    str_detect(term, "^same_region")    ~ "same_region",
    str_detect(term, "^cust_region")    ~ "customer_zip_region",
    str_detect(term, "^seller_region")  ~ "seller_zip_region",
    str_detect(term, "^purchase_year")  ~ "purchase_year",
    str_detect(term, "^purchase_month") ~ "purchase_month",
    str_detect(term, "^purchase_dow")   ~ "purchase_weekday",
    str_detect(term, "^category")       ~ "product_category",
    TRUE ~ term
  )) |>
  group_by(feature) |>
  summarise(importance = sum(importance), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(share = importance / sum(importance)) |>
  arrange(desc(importance))

Decision tree importance, summed across dummy columns (Recipe 3)








Route features carry the most importance. Customer and seller state, the same-state and same-region flags, and the zip regions together account for 53% of the tree’s importance. The three most important single features are customer_state (18%), same_state (17%), and estimated_days (14%); estimated_days is Olist’s own estimate, which itself partly reflects the route.
Purchase timing contributes a smaller share (10% for year, month, and weekday combined), well below route but not zero. The Exploration page found that purchase month moves average delivery time by several days while weekday and time of day barely matter. This importance score cannot show which months matter, so we do not name them here.
estimated_days ranks high in importance but added little to accuracy. The tree uses it often, but because route features carry much of the same information, removing it costs little. Importance measures how much a feature is used; the recipe comparison measures how much accuracy it adds.
Caution: correlated features share credit in tree importance, and neither the lasso nor the tree shows causation. These results describe what the models rely on to predict, not what causes a delay.
